en: Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty,
recorded by his disciple Guanding:
Furthermore, one should contemplate that throughout immeasurable kalpas, [beings] have mostly been bound by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as well as perception and mental formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra*).
Regarding the calculation of self and person:
if one clings to the notion of agency and suddenly hears praise or abuse,
thinking, "They are praising or abusing me."
In all activities—standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—one regards every object as "I.
It is like having glue on one's hands; whatever one grasps adheres to it.
As the Sūtra says:
It is impossible for an ordinary person to be free from the notion of a self.
Even when encountering poverty and losing their original resolve,
they still continue to conceive of a self without ceasing.
If one attains wealth and nobility, they will indulge in power and let loose poison, cruelly harming the world;
with fierce rage and great prosperity, they will wrong the innocent.
All such karmic actions that arise are considered by them to be their own doing.
Who would dare to take its place?
If one holds a torch against the wind, how could it fail to burn one's hand?
It is like mistaking a room at night for a haunted house.
When the clear light of dawn shines forth, it is simply one's original self;
yet, because there is no wisdom, one recklessly asserts that there is a "self.
When observed with true insight, however, there is in fact no self at all.
"I am in what place?
Thus he minutely observes each and every part— the head, feet, and limbs—
and finds no "self" whatsoever.
Wherein are there any persons or sentient beings?
The mechanism of karmic power is but a provisional empty village;
born from a multitude of conditions, it has no sovereign master.
It is like two ghosts disputing over a corpse in an empty pavilion overnight;
when one contemplates in this manner, the delusion of self ceases.
If one cultivates the four contemplations, the four inversions are destroyed.
The mind of the Way arose with intense vigor, giving rise to great fear.
It was as if pursued by an enemy, as if fleeing from a hostile land,
or as if traveling a perilous path, trembling in every thought and seeking only an escape.
When the deer hears the hunt and the surrounding encirclement, it flees in utter terror;
even upon encountering water or grass, it has no leisure to drink or eat,
for its sole intent is to escape.
The śrāvakas are like this:
if a deer breaks through the enclosure and narrowly escapes disaster,
it gallops away while repeatedly looking back.
He wailed and sobbed, pained by his longing for his original herd;
yet though he hesitated, he knew it would be of no further avail.
Suppressing his breath and stifling his voice, he moved forward while harboring his grief.
The Pratyekabuddhas are likewise.
Having emerged from birth and death, they take pity on sentient beings;
yet, though they feel profound sorrow and lamentation, they are unable to rescue or deliver them.
Even though the Great Elephant King heard that they were surrounded, he could not bear to leave his son alone;
knowing his own strength was sufficient to withstand swords and arrows,
he protected his offspring so that the herd might remain safe and escape harm.
So it is with the Bodhisattva:
when the clear contemplations of impermanence and non-self arise,
their mind is so pierced by fear that it is as if they were treading upon water or fire.
Furthermore, he gives rise to compassion, thinking of sentient beings as a mother thinks of her child:
"Sentient beings are blind and ignorant, unaware that they are being scorched by suffering;
how could I now abandon them and depart alone?"
They endure birth and death;
through wisdom and skillful means, they teach and mature others, creating the conditions for their liberation.
Their own merits, dharma-body, and life of wisdom increase ever further.
When the conditions are met and the capacity for enlightenment has ripened, one immediately sits at the site of awakening and attains Buddhahood.
Together with all sentient beings, one emerges from the three realms of existence,
just as that great elephant brings peace to both itself and others.
Just as a young elephant cub, though it may parry swords and arrows,
will inevitably be pierced by them to the detriment of both itself and others,
so too is the bodhisattva at the initial stage who wishes to enter the cycle of birth and death.
Upon contact with birth and death, one loses and regresses from the roots of goodness and the dharmakāya is destroyed.
Nevertheless, the merit of generating the mind of great compassion is praiseworthy;
thus, although bodhisattvas fear birth and death, [they do not abandon it].
They constantly seek the roots of goodness to bear the burden of sentient beings,
differing from those of the two vehicles;
though they abide within birth and death, they do not crave the five desires.
It is only because they act for the sake of universal salvation that they differ from ordinary people.
As a sutra says:
"They do not abide in discipline, nor do they abide in non-discipline."
Although he knows there is no self, he teaches others without weariness;
although he knows nirvana, he does not enter final extinction;
although he knows impurity, he does not speak of revulsion.
This is precisely that meaning.
Extensively cultivating the roots of goodness through the merit of the six perfections is like the body of a sheep becoming fat.
Diligently contemplating that all evil karmas are subject to destruction,
one is constantly terrified by the wolf like a fatless sheep;
this is called the characteristic of practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Whether practicing it oneself or teaching others to praise the Dharma and those who praise it, one invokes the Buddhas of the ten directions as witnesses and saviors.
Through the majestic empowerment of all Buddhas, one is freed from obstacles and attains liberation,
thereby becoming endowed with the four kinds of tenfold wisdom.
This is like using oil as an aid to increase the light of the Way, and so forth.
If one lacks both rational contemplation and ritual repentance,
yet rashly hopes for the Buddha’s seal of approval to seek profit and pursue fame.
If one were to seal this with the Buddha, such a thing would be impossible.
If one contemplates the principle without interruption, borrowing phenomena to break through obscurations,
this is the true mental confession.
This seal marks this place.
The reason one must rely on those who assist in the Way is like the jewel fastened at the neck by twenty trillion Buddhas.
If one forgets the Mahāyāna in the interim, they will not be transformed by the Great [Vehicle].
For another six hundred kalpas, they are led by means of the Small [Vehicle] to arouse [the aspiration for awakening],
causing them to fear birth and death and gradually turn toward their father’s house.
Thus we know that the small should be borrowed to assist the great.
Furthermore, when the Buddha first desired to bring about a great transformation, the Buddhas did not approve;
however, once he contemplated skillful means, they immediately exclaimed, "Excellent! (Sādhu).
It is like the son of a wealthy family who is ill and should take Yellow Dragon Decoction;
how could his parents begrudge him such excellent medicine?
They should simply encourage him to take it.
Having taken the medicine, his illness was cured.
The Buddha has a fundamental vow to cause all beings to become like himself;
how could he begrudge the Mahāyāna?
Having no choice but to act, he adapts to the capacities of beings as an antidote;
the opening of the gate for the path of assistance is likewise in this sense.
Question: If the cultivation of the samādhis that assist the path is not accomplished,
should the six perfections not be superior to the factors of enlightenment?
Answer: There are three propositions here:
the six perfections subvert the categories of the path, and the categories of the path subvert the six perfections.
In the "Chapter on Cultivating the Six Perfections," one cultivates the six perfections within the chapter on the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*).
The six perfections are the path-factors, and the path-factors are the six perfections.
As mentioned above, if these path-factors cannot accord with reality, [they are not the true path].
If one cultivates the six perfections, one is able to destroy obscurations;
is it not then the case that the six perfections destroy the factors of the path?
At times, however, the six perfections may fail to reach the other shore.
If one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas), one immediately attains realization;
this constitutes the factors of enlightenment subverting the six perfections.
If one cultivates the six perfections...
First, one destroys the six obscurations;

then, by advancing in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas), they will be spontaneously accomplished. This constitutes the six perfections as the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.
As stated above, this is precisely the cultivation of the six perfections within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Regarding how the six perfections and the factors of enlightenment are mutually identical:
Dāna is itself the Mahāyāna;
the four foundations of mindfulness are also themselves the Mahāyāna.
Dāna and the factors of enlightenment are non-dual and without distinction.
Because they are unattainable.
Generally speaking, among all phenomena, those that are of no benefit to practice mutually negate one another,
while those that are beneficial to practice mutually cultivate one another.
In terms of principle, they are mutually identical.
Whether regarding the Four Truths or dependent origination, existence and non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence—
extensively applied to all phenomena— each possesses these three aspects.
If one attains this mastery of mind, one may speak at length as follows.
What is the meaning of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) subduing the sense faculties?
It is that the six sense organs do not receive the six sense objects.
This corresponds to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) among the factors of the path;
it is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) that disciplines the faculties.

When the six sense organs are not harmed by the six objects of perception, this corresponds to right action (*samyak-karmānta*), right speech (*samyag-vāk*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) among the factors of the path.
This is precisely the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) that subdues the sense faculties.

To remain unshaken through patient endurance (*kṣānti*) despite the six sense objects that conflict with one's inclinations is to accord with the four kinds of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) that subdues the sense faculties.
Guarding the faculties and their objects while remaining constantly untiring is precisely what accords with the eightfold diligence of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
This is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) in subduing the sense faculties;
with a concentrated mind that is undisturbed and not deluded by the six sense objects,
one immediately accords with the eightfold concentration of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
This is called the perfection of dhyāna (meditation) that subdues the sense faculties;
it consists in knowing that the six sense objects are impermanent, suffering, empty, and quiescent,
which is precisely the unification with the ten kinds of wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that tames the sense faculties.
This constitutes the fulfillment of the six perfections through the taming of the sense faculties according to the Tripitaka.
Furthermore, one knows that the eye is empty and does not grasp at the eye.
Form is empty and does not receive form,
because the sense faculties and their objects are empty;
this is called the practice of constant relinquishment.
Even unto the emptiness of the mind, one does not grasp at the mind;
the emptiness of phenomena, wherein one does not grasp at phenomena, is called the practice of constant relinquishment.
This is precisely the factor of enlightenment of equanimity within the factors of the path.
This is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) that tames the sense faculties.
The emptiness of form cannot harm the emptiness of the eye;
the emptiness of the eye cannot harm the emptiness of form.
Even up to the point that the emptiness of phenomena finds no opportunity against the mind, and the emptiness of the mind finds no opportunity against phenomena;
this is precisely the convergence of the factors of enlightenment: right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
This is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) that tames all the sense faculties.
Furthermore, because the eye and forms are empty,
there is neither opposition nor compliance, neither patience nor impatience.
Up to and including the emptiness of mind and mental objects (*dharmas*),
there is neither opposition nor compliance, neither patience nor impatience;
this is precisely the unification with the four kinds of mindfulness belonging to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*).
This is called the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) that tames all the sense faculties.
The eye and forms are eternally empty; there is no time when they are not empty.
Thus, one should practice and respond in accordance with this, being in union with prajñā.
Even unto the mind and mental phenomena, they are eternally empty and never not empty;
this is called being in accord with Prajñā.
It is precisely the unification with the eightfold diligence of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
This is called the perfection of vigor that subdues the sense faculties:
because the eye and forms are empty, there is no distraction and no attachment;
and so on, up to: because the mind and mental objects are empty, there is no distraction and no attachment.
This is the unification with the various concentrations of the factors of enlightenment;
it is called the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) that tames the sense faculties.
Because the eye and forms are empty, one is neither deluded nor wise.
Up to and including the fact that because mind and mental objects (*dharmas*) are empty, there is neither delusion nor wisdom;
this is precisely the unification with the ten kinds of wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*).
This is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) taming all the sense faculties.
This refers to the Shared Teaching (Pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna), which subdues the various faculties and fulfills the six perfections.
If the eye and form encompass the ten dharma-realms,
each of these ten dharma-realms possesses its own distinct fruit-retribution, varying in terms of superiority and inferiority.
Each cultivates causes with varying degrees of depth;
thus, cause and effect are immeasurable and inexhaustible.
One must set aside ignorant conceptualization of dharmic characteristics and remain free from any grasping or attachment.
Even unto the mind and mental objects, one possesses the non-attachment that discriminates the ten dharma-realms;
this is precisely the integration of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) and the awakening factor of equanimity.
This is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) that subdues the sense faculties.
He discriminates the immeasurable characteristics of everything from the eye and forms up to the mind and mental objects;
he never fails to accord with the capacities of others, thereby harming their roots of goodness,
nor does he himself suffer injury from the immeasurable sense faculties and their objects.
That is to say, it unites with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), namely right action, speech, and livelihood;
this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) that subdues the sense faculties.
Furthermore, regarding the ten realms of sense organs and their objects, whether they are adverse or favorable, [one remains equanimous].
With a mind unmoving and dwelling securely within the conventional, one is able to endure and accomplish the work of the Path;
this is the unification with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) and mindfulness.
This is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) that subdues all the sense faculties.
Furthermore, when discerning all sense faculties and their objects,
even if difficult or painful thoughts arise,
one must not retreat midway.
To possess courage amidst birth and death is precisely the diligence that accords with the factors of enlightenment;
this is called the perfection of vigor that subdues the sense faculties.
Furthermore, when one discriminates all faculties and objects while the mind remains undisturbed, unagitated, and unbiased,
it is then in accord with the various meditative concentrations of the factors of enlightenment.
This is called the perfection of dhyāna that subdues the sense faculties.
Furthermore, by discerning all faculties and objects,
one bestows appropriate medicine through the power of knowledge regarding the various paths and their elements.
Skillful means are likewise free from attachment;
this is the integration of all wisdoms within the factors of enlightenment.
This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that subdues the sense faculties.
This refers to the Separate Teaching (pr̥thag-dharma), which subdues the various faculties and fulfills the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
Furthermore, as stated in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*:
"That eye-faculty is, with respect to all Tathāgatas, eternal."
Those who possess the complete and undiminished cultivation and see with perfect clarity and distinction,
these are the eye-faculties of the nine dharma-realms.
Regarding the permanence of the Tathāgata:
the nine elements each claim that they themselves are not real;
the Tathāgata, however, observes them thus.
That is to say, the Buddha-dharmadhātu is non-dual and undifferentiated.
For one who practices without diminution,
they contemplate all eyes as the Buddha-eye.
The perfect cause, consisting of the three truths within a single mind, is fully complete without any deficiency.
For one who perceives with clear and distinct understanding:
to perceive the Real is "clearly seeing," and to perceive the Provisional is "distinctly seeing."
The three wisdoms are fully present within a single mind, wherein the five eyes are complete and illuminate all-pervasively;
this is called "clearly seeing the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the vision, it is the perfect realization; regarding the treatise, it is the perfect cause.
Furthermore, for one who practices with full completion:
contemplating the faculty of the eye and relinquishing the outflows of the two extremes is called *dāna* (generosity).
That the faculty of the eye is not harmed by the two extremes is called *śīla* (ethical discipline).
The quiescence of the eye-faculty, unmoved by the two extremes, is called *kṣānti*.
The spontaneous entry of the eye-faculty and its consciousness into the ocean of *sarvajñatā* is called *vīrya*.
To contemplate the true nature of the eye is called the supreme concentration;
to illuminate the middle way within the eye with the knowledge of all modes is called wisdom.
This is the cultivation of the eye faculty in its fullness, without deficiency.
Because it is without decrease, one sees the dharma-realm of the eye with perfect clarity;
likewise, regarding that mental faculty, one knows with perfect clarity that it is always fully endowed and without decrease in its cultivation toward all Tathāgatas.
In each and every faculty, there is emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;
these three contemplations within a single mind are called "unfailing cultivation.
One realizes the wisdom-eye, the dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye by attaining them within this single mind.
This is called "clearly seeing," as described above.
Just as the faculties are thus, so too are the objects.
All dharmas are likewise so. This is the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) that subdues the faculties and fulfills the six perfections.
This is ultimate subduing and ultimate fulfillment.
In this way, one should know that the six perfections, which assist the path and the ultimate path, are universally capable of subduing all the faculties.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
Because the giver, the receiver, and the material gift cannot be apprehended,
one fulfills the dāna-pāramitā.
Having transcended these three factors and being without attachment, this is precisely the essence of dāna.
One should be fully endowed.
To practice the two kinds of giving—of material wealth and of the Dharma—is called being "endowed. This signifies the perfection of both the phenomenal and the noumenal.
It is called "complete" because it benefits both oneself and others:
in terms of practice, it breaks through stinginess regarding material things so that one can relinquish wealth;
in terms of principle, it breaks through stinginess regarding the Dharma so that one can relinquish the teachings.
When both [the afflictions and the objects] are destroyed and both [the body and the requisites] are relinquished, yet the essence and the implements are fully perfected, it is called a *pāramitā*.
How do the six perfections encompass the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) of a Buddha?
The Buddha takes the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth, as his majestic deportment.
Cultivating the four factors of enlightenment within a single mind is called practicing the Buddha’s majestic demeanor (*īryāpatha*);
realizing the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom is called attaining the Buddha’s majestic demeanor.
Now, following the flow of the discourse, I shall clarify how the ten powers (*daśabala*) are subsumed by means of the factors of enlightenment.
If the fourfold path-factors are indeed the fourfold knowledge of the Four Noble Truths as the certainty of cause and effect,
then it is possible that one who knows the accumulation of arising and ceasing will certainly undergo the suffering of the three realms.
It is impossible that the accumulation of arising and ceasing could reach the nirvana without remainder;
it is possible that the path of arising and ceasing can exhaust suffering and enter nirvana.
If the path of arising and ceasing were to reach the three realms, such a thing is impossible.
Even if it were to reach the accumulation of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and extend to the transformation of support (*pariṇāmiki-vipariṇāma*), such a thing is possible.
If it were to extend to unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, such a thing is impossible.
If the unconditioned path of cessation extends universally to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), this is possible;
if it extends only to the two vehicles, this is impossible.
These four causes and effects are known, decisively judged, clearly understood, and definitively severed within a single moment of mind.
This is called the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar within the Buddha-dharma:
"Only in my teaching are there the four fruits of the śramaṇa."
This is precisely that meaning.
Regarding the power of knowledge of the results of karma:
knowing the four kinds of accumulation is what constitutes the knowledge of karma.
To know suffering is to know retribution;
the same applies to the Path and Cessation.
One discerns the four types of karmic retribution according to their depth and shallowness without error.
These are the two powers.
Regarding the power of knowing the concentration of dhyāna:
it refers to the eight concentrations within the fourfold Truth of the Path.
To discern the depths and shallows with unerring clarity—
this is the third power.
As for the power of knowing the faculties, desires, and dispositions:
Knowing that the past suffering and its origin differ is called the power of faculty (*indriya*);
knowing that the present suffering and its origin differ in terms of aspiration is called the power of desire (*chanda*);
knowing that the future suffering and its origin differ in terms of attainment and loss is called the power of nature (*bhāva*).
These are the fourth, fifth, and sixth powers.
Regarding the power of knowing the path leading to the destination:
it is the knowledge of the destination reached by means of the four truths of the path.
These are the seven powers.
Regarding the power of knowing past lives and the divine eye:
it illuminates the good and evil natures, as well as the long and short lifespans, across one lifetime or many lifetimes in the past.

The power to know past lives is called the power of recollecting former existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*). The power that illuminates the beauty or ugliness of future places of birth is called the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurjñānabala*).
These are called the eight and nine powers (*bala*).
As for the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayabala*), it is the untainted mind and wisdom, along with liberation, realized through the fourfold Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Regarding how this single Dharma-gate has four aspects:
it is like a king’s secret speech that a wise minister understands;
thus, the Buddha’s teaching of the ten powers accords with four types of capacities.
It does not allow the small to slander the great and thereby harm their merit;
nor does it allow the great to disparage the small and thereby suppress their roots of goodness.
Each individual hears [the teaching] alone and each attains benefit accordingly.
Because he possesses no contrived expedients, he is called Śākyamuni.
The Bodhisattva, as a wise minister, deeply understands esoteric speech;
knowing that the intention lay within the Tripitaka, he immediately inquired about arising and ceasing.
Consult with gravity so that those with the karmic affinity may awaken swiftly;
even to the point of knowing that the intent lies in the Perfect [Teaching].
Whether chanting on non-action or inquiring about non-action.
It enables others to attain understanding;
with a single voice, it proclaims diverse teachings so that all who hear rejoice.
The meaning of the secret of speech is boundless and inexhaustible.
Since the preceding four explanations have been provided, why should one harbor any doubt?
Question: The ten powers (daśabala) are the majestic deportment of a Buddha;
how can a beginner study them, and how can they attain them?
Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"A bodhisattva practicing prajñā should not dwell upon the ten powers or the fearlessnesses."
If the Buddha were without fault regarding the Buddha-dharma, then he would indeed abide [in it].
But if the Bodhisattva lacks the Buddha-dharma, what could be discussed regarding his abiding?
The commentary states:
When a bodhisattva cultivates the merits of a Buddha, they often give rise to a heavy attachment;
it is to destroy this sense of weightiness that it is said one "should not dwell" [upon them].
Furthermore, the bodhisattva partially attains the ten powers and the fearlessnesses.
Since it has not yet been perfected, one should not abide therein.
If that is so, although one previously practiced it, one has not yet attained it.
How can later discourse on entering the stages be relevant to the initial resolve?

If one follows the "Ten Abodes Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it says that because a bodhisattva attains a portion of the ten powers through their initial generation of the mind, the deity *Samyaksmṛti* asks *Dharmamati*: [text continues]
How does a bodhisattva of initial resolve cultivate the skillful means of the ten powers?
How does one know that the household life is not the home and thus leave home to study the Way?
By what skillful means does one cultivate the holy life, fulfill the path of the ten abodes, and swiftly attain Bodhi?
The answer says:
A bodhisattva should first distinguish ten kinds of dharmas, namely:
the three types of action, as well as the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts.
If the body were the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
the holy life would be turbid with eighty thousand families of worms.
If bodily action (*kāyakarman*) were the holy life...
In the four modes of deportment— whether looking around, raising or lowering the feet,
or when the mouth performs the Brahma-faring—
the sounds touch the mind as the lips, teeth, and tongue move.
If verbal karma were the holy life (brahmacarya), it would be mere speech;
and so on, up to: if ethical discipline were the holy life.
The boundary for the precept platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*); the ten-member assembly inquiring into purity;
the preceptor’s formal announcement (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) regarding the shaving of the hair, begging for alms, and so forth.
All these are not the holy life (brahmacarya). Where does the holy life reside?
Who possesses the holy life?
The equality of the three periods of time, which is like space,
is called skillful means.
Furthermore, one further cultivates ten superior dharmas.
These so-called ten powers are profound and immeasurable.
One who contemplates them in this way will swiftly attain all the merits of the Buddhas.
At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening;
knowing the true nature of all phenomena, one is fully endowed with the body of wisdom and realizes it through no other means.
Is such an explicit statement not [proof] that the ten powers are realized through cultivation from the very beginning?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The Bodhisattva knows the Tathāgatagarbha."
Having heard and contemplated the preliminaries, one cultivates the nature of meditation;
thereby, one gains entry into all meditations.
There are three types of all meditations.
First, there is happiness in the present life;
because it is happiness in the present life, it is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Second, there is the production of the lineage of the ten powers (*daśabala-gotra*), as well as the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) of the two vehicles.
The third is the dhyāna for benefiting sentient beings.
The ten abodes (bhūmis) are called the wisdom of hearing;
the ten practices (caryās) are called the wisdom of reflection.
Having previously cultivated the intrinsic nature through hearing and reflection,
one enters all meditative absorptions and attains the three dharmas;
is this not cultivation and realization from the very first moment?
The third point is clear.
The factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣa*), the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśa-bala*) encompass one another through their mutual interrelation,
all as explained above.
If one cultivates the six perfections as the factors of the path,
this is itself the cultivation of the Buddha’s ten powers;
if one subdues the sense faculties and fulfills the six perfections, [this is likewise so].
This means that one fulfills the ten powers (*daśabala*) and abides in the majestic demeanor (*īryāpatha*) of a Buddha without distinction.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"Power (*bala*) is named for its assistance; its vital strength (*vīrya-bala*) is inexhaustible."
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Attaining superior capability is called power (*bala*).
Regarding the ten points, being entirely in accordance with reality and free from falsehood is superior to Māra."

nor is it the discriminating eye of the bodhisattvas.
It is solely the Buddha-eye, which possesses the five powers.
Just as when various rivers flow into the ocean they lose their original names,
the Buddha asked Subhūti:
"Does the Tathāgata possess the five eyes?"
The answer was:
"There is. All [who speak] refer to it as the Tathāgata having [it].
What concern does this have for the eyes of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles?
As the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* states:
"One attains bodhi by being fully endowed with the five eyes."
To unify the three contemplations within a single mind is called the cultivation of non-decrease.
To possess the five powers within a single eye is called the gate of clear vision for entering;
it is also the realization of perfection.
Having attained mastery over the internal and external eye,
one enters the meditative absorption of the eye and emerges from the samādhi of the nose; one enters the meditative absorption of the nose and emerges from the eye.
Though moving, it is quiescent; quiescence does not obstruct movement.
Though quiescent, it moves; movement does not obstruct quiescence.
Though seeing, it is non-seeing; through non-seeing, there is seeing.
Thus it is said that he clearly saw [the man] entering the gate.
Question:
The Buddha possesses the five eyes and should therefore illumine the five objects of perception.
The Sūtra says:
"With my five eyes, I do not see sentient beings of the three categories;
how could those who are mad, foolish, and sightless claim to see?"
It is further said:
"Seeing forms is equal to being blind. Since it is equal to being blind, [how can there be seeing?]
Question: How can one perceive coarse and subtle forms? Answer:
The five sense objects are all identical with the true reality (dharmatā).
Since true reality cannot be seen, [the objects] cannot be seen either.
Because it is invisible, it is likened to being blind; yet,
though it is invisible, its capacity for seeing is not diminished in the slightest,
as the five eyes penetrate all objects with perfect clarity.
Although it is said that the five types of vision must exist for illumination to occur,
although it is said that one is blind, being blind does not necessarily mean there is no sight at all.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"To come without the characteristic of coming;
to see without the characteristic of seeing"—
this is precisely the meaning of this.
This is the inconceivable realm.
My eye and the eyes of sentient beings are neither two nor distinct.
Why, then, do sentient beings fail to awaken to this and remain ignorant?
Immediately giving rise to compassion, he vowed to deliver and liberate [all beings].
Wishing to fulfill this vow, he settled his mind in concentration and wisdom,
and was able to universally dismantle all phenomena through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Within the eye and forms, one clearly discerns their penetration and obstruction,
unlike the path of insects;
within the aggregate of the eye, one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness as being neither pure nor impure.
Having cast off both decay and flourishing, one enters nirvana.

By studying various antidotes, one assists in opening the three gates of liberation and clearly discerns the six stages of realization, so that arrogance and presumption do not arise. Though my eye of contemplation possesses the five eyes, it is complete in its function.
However, these are merely names and merely contemplative practices.
If one gradually perceives what is beyond the obstruction and subsequently perceives the ten directions,
it is as described in the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra*.
Suddenly I see the great trichiliocosm as it was for Sadāparibhūta;
gradually and suddenly I see the six sense faculties functioning interchangeably.
Since I have not yet attained these stages, I should not give rise to arrogance, but should instead feel gradual remorse and practice with diligence.
If virtue is established and renown attained,
one should endure internal and external obstacles as steadfastly as Mount Sumeru;
when attachment to the Dharma does not arise, there will be no lingering hindrance.
Swift as the wind, it realizes the eye of truth;
riding upon a great carriage, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment.
If one gains entry through the eye, one performs extensive Buddha-works within that very eye.
It constantly emits golden light that illuminates all things.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"There are some buddha-fields where light constitutes the Buddha-work. Since this is the case for the single reception of visual form by the eye, it is so for the others as well.
The same applies to the other two feelings.
The same applies to the remaining five faculties, the five objects, and the fifteen feelings;
as explained in detail previously.
Apply the preceding intent by entering it into the six sense faculties;
simply cause the destruction of afflictions and do not be constrained by conventional rules.
If one attains the Great Vehicle through the ears, [one shall attain liberation].
He frequently employs sounds as a Buddha-activity;
he uses fragrance through the nose and flavors through the tongue;
he uses celestial robes for the body and tranquility for the mind.
The Buddha-activity of a single faculty interpenetrates all faculties.
While the skillful means employed to benefit sentient beings may at times differ,
they cause all beings to attain ultimate bliss, and so forth.
If one can practice diligently as described above,
this single lifetime will certainly not be spent in vain. Though one may hear these teachings,
if they are not put into practice, it is like a black viper carrying a jewel within its coils.
What benefit does this bring to a long serpent?
Now, I shall employ three analogies to illustrate gain and loss.
A common man of singular valor refines a single sword and a single arrow.
For every one or two enemies defeated, he receives a reward of one gold and one silver ingot;
his emolument benefits his wife and son.
Such a person values only his weapons and implements.
Carrying halberds as vanguard to command the acquisition of goods—
how could such a person be of use for broad knowledge of the art of war?
If one wishes to serve as the yeast and malt for a nation, as oars and rudders, as salt and vinegar, or as a drenching rain, [one must possess these qualities].
One must be proficient in both civil and military arts;
when strategy is deliberated within the curtains and screens, one can repel threats from ten thousand *li* away.
What is learned therein is profound, and what is overcome thereby is likewise vast.
Having received such heavy rewards and abundant stipends, though he knew [the truth], he did not employ it;
and having employed it, he was repeatedly defeated in the north. If he could not even save himself, how could his grace possibly reach others?
It is the same for those who study meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*):
they know only a single method, whether it be calming (*śamatha*) or insight (*vipaśyanā*), intending to destroy minor evils and practice the Path with a tranquil mind;
they attain a small measure of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and gather a small circle of followers.
He then considers this sufficient;
it is merely like a commoner’s quarrel.
Yet he wishes to become a great Chan master to shatter the great afflictions.
To manifest immeasurable wholesome dharmas and to benefit immeasurable conditions,
one should study the ten dharmas for the sake of thoroughly penetrating the intent of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Regarding the six objects, there is the application of the six types of feeling in accordance with their functions.
When afflictions suddenly arise, one immediately engages in contemplation.
By contemplating the faults of delusions, one manifests valor in difficult tasks, like untying a topknot to retrieve a jewel.
If one understands but does not apply it, or applies it inappropriately,
how can one overcome the delusions of the mind through the Way?
It is like a wild sorcerer who understands only a single technique.
If one merely seeks to save a single person and obtain a single platter of dried meat, why is there any need to study Shen Nong’s *Bencao*?

One who wishes to act as a great physician must peruse all treatments and extensively heal various ailments; thus, one turns the pulse until it becomes refined, and applies remedies until their efficacy is repeatedly verified.
His grace in saving others is vast.
It is the same for those who study Chan:
simply by focusing single-mindedly on one method, delusions will depart.
At that time, such slight benefit was ultimately not the intended meaning of encompassing the Great Path (mahāmārga).
Furthermore, it could not destroy afflictions (*kleśa*) or lead one into the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It is like being skilled in medicine yet failing to take it according to the prescribed formula.
"How can the illness possibly be cured?
Although your recitation and practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are very proficient,
because your mind does not apply them in practice, the realization of non-arising will never manifest before you."
Furthermore, if one merely wishes to engage in the practice of debate, answering a single question with a single response for the sake of momentary display,
why is it necessary to extensively seek out the sūtras and śāstras?
However, if one wishes to act as a master of the Dharma, one must be proficient in the various schools (nikāyas).
Although you have mastered many points of doctrine, you have never stepped forward among the assembly;
out of timidity, you are unable to respond to challenges.
If you were free from fear, you could turn your responses a hundredfold according to the occasion with unimpeded answers.
One who answers questions posed from any direction is called a Great Dharma Master;
the practitioner of contemplation is likewise so.
If contemplative practice is clear, one will be able to apply it at every opportunity and in response to every object encountered. If it is not so,
by what means can the armies of Māra be destroyed?
By what means can the grave illness of the afflictions be eliminated?
By what means can the profound meaning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) be revealed?
If these three tasks remain unaccomplished, one will labor in vain under weary toil.
This is merely the state of an ordinary person caught in birth and death;
it is not the expedient means for studying the Way.
